artificial intelligence; the capability of a computer or other machine to perform tasks normally associated with human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, language processing and recognizing patterns; also the field and technologies concerned with creating such systems
x: Bedriften bruker AI til å analysere store datamengder.
The company uses AI to analyze large amounts of data.
Selv synes han det mest skremmende med AI spesielt og den teknologiske utviklingen generelt, er hvordan automatiseringen av «kunnskapsarbeid» […]
He himself thinks the most frightening thing about AI in particular, and technological development in general, is the automation of “knowledge work” […]

1000195.etyen:
First attested in 1983 in Norwegian. Unadapted borrowing from English AI (“artificial intelligence”), an initialism of artificial intelligence. The English term artificial intelligence was coined in 1955 by John McCarthy.
English artificial is from Middle English artificial (“artificial, man-made”), from Old French artificial, from Latin artificiālis (“artificial”), from Latin artificium (“art, craft, skill”), ultimately involving ars (“art, skill, craft”) and facere (“to make, do”). ars ultimately derives from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to fit, join”), while facere ultimately derives from P

en.g: a female given name from English [in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], equivalent to English Ann

1000451.etyen:
Borrowed from English Ann (“female given name”) in much of its modern use; independently also an e-less Norwegian form of Anne, particularly in older regional usage. Both developments ultimately go back to Late Latin Anna (“female given name”), from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “Hannah; grace, favour”), from Biblical Hebrew חָנַן (ḥānan, “to be gracious, show favour”).
Compare Danish Ann and Swedish Ann (“female given name”), both likewise borrowed from English.

1004035.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂ōwyóm
From a- (“first or best in rank or quality”) + egg (“egg”).
The first element is a- (“first or best in rank or quality”), from the use of the letter A (“A”) to denote the first or highest rank or quality. The second element, egg (“egg”), is inherited from Old Norse egg n (“egg”), from Proto-Germanic *ajją (“egg”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”).

a surname from skank (“leg, shank”), borne by several Norwegian families, including an old and widely branched noble family traditionally associated with Jämtland

1004547.etyen:
From the common noun skank (“leg, shank”), ultimately from Old Norse skankr (“leg, shank”). The surname was probably taken from the family's heraldic emblem, which depicts an armoured leg, and is therefore likely a heraldic surname based on the charge in the coat of arms. The family's earlier origin is uncertain, although it is traditionally associated with Jämtland.
Compare Danish skank, Swedish skank, English shank and German Schenkel (“leg, shank”).
